Field surveys of African Sleeper populations in coastal West African lagoons have documented that females ultimately attain a maximum total length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], a size that reflects the moderate growth potential of this eleotrid species. Newly emerged prolarvae from demersal, adhesive eggs measure approximately 1.8 millimeters in egg diameter, and upon hatching the yolk-sac larva possesses a wet weight at birth of just 0.000087 grams [Wwb = 0.000087 grams], reflecting the minute energetic reserves packaged within the chorionated embryo. This extraordinarily low birth mass is consistent with the pelagic larval phase typical of many eleotrids, where initial endotrophic development relies entirely on yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The species occupies brackish waters and vegetated margins, and growth rates appear strongly influenced by local prey availability and water temperature. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the ultimate length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters] places Bostrychus africanus at an intermediate position within the genus, between smaller marsh-dwelling forms and larger fluvial specialists.

Reproductive maturation in Bostrychus africanus occurs at a relatively modest body size, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of approximately 10 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10 centimeters], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of around 7.2 grams [Wwp = around 7.2 grams]. This length at sexual maturation represents roughly half the ultimate body length of adult females, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous fishes where reproductive activity commences well before somatic growth ceases. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation is triggered by seasonal cues, and field collections indicate that gravid individuals are most frequently encountered during the rainy season when flooded littoral zones provide abundant spawning habitat. The relationship between length and mass at maturation follows a power function derived from a condition factor of 0.00646, with the weight at puberty being considerably lower than the ultimate adult mass. This developmental schedule ensures that individuals can begin contributing to the next generation while still devoting substantial resources to continued somatic expansion.

The maximum reproductive output of Bostrychus africanus was evaluated under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], reflecting the thermal regime of its native habitat during the peak spawning season. Under these conditions, females produce approximately 23,479 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 23,479 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring once per year [F_R_i = once per year]. This sustained reproductive effort is supported by a high assimilation efficiency, allowing continuous oocyte recruitment even during periods of moderate food availability. The combination of a large clutch size with low spawning frequency yields a substantial annual reproductive output, a strategy well suited to an environment where early life stages face considerable mortality from predation and variable physicochemical conditions. The reproductive rate is notably high for an eleotrid of this body size, exceeding values reported for several related species with similar life histories.

Field records indicate that the maximum lifespan of Bostrychus africanus is approximately three years [am = approximately three years] when maintained at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C], the thermal conditions typical of its natural range. This relatively short longevity is characteristic of small to medium-sized tropical eleotrids, many of which exhibit fast growth, early maturation, and high reproductive investment at the expense of extended somatic persistence. Senescent individuals captured in lagoon systems show progressive deterioration of fin condition and reduced feeding efficiency, suggesting that physiological decline accelerates after the second breeding season. The lifespan of approximately three years [am = approximately three years] at 26.5 °C [T = 26.5 °C] represents a complete life cycle from fertilized ovum through multiple reproductive episodes to eventual natural mortality, with most individuals completing two or three spawning seasons before succumbing to age-related physiological decline. Comparative data from congeneric species in cooler thermal regimes suggest that lifespan may be extended at lower temperatures.

The ultimate wet weight of adult female Bostrychus africanus reaches approximately 70 grams [Wwi = approximately 70 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this population. This asymptotic body mass is achieved after the growth rate decelerates markedly following the onset of reproductive activity, with most somatic expansion occurring during the juvenile and early adult phases. In comparison to the wet weight at puberty of around 7.2 grams, the ultimate wet weight represents nearly a tenfold increase in body mass between maturation and full adult size, underscoring the substantial post-pubertal growth capacity of this species. The length-weight scaling exponent of approximately 3.05 indicates a slightly positive allometric relationship, meaning that larger individuals become proportionally heavier relative to their length, likely reflecting enhanced condition and greater energy reserves in mature adults. This body mass trajectory is consistent with a life history strategy that balances early reproduction with continued somatic investment across multiple breeding seasons.
